title: Precepts Intro
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The precepts in Soto Zen are not meant to be a rigid set of rules, but rather a guiding framework for living a compassionate and mindful life that supports spiritual growth. Developed from the Tendai school's adoption of Chinese Bodhisattva precepts, these 16 guidelines emphasize connection, humility, and generosity, encouraging practitioners to honor their ancestors and cultivate a sense of community and social responsibility. By embracing this approach, Soto Zen practitioners aim to embody the principles of compassion and wisdom in all aspects of life.

sentences.text: So we'll start tonight a series of talks on the precepts, the ethical precepts of Zen.
The main theme of this introductory talk is that the way they're understood in the tradition has a much broader meaning than just a list of things to do.
We say "ethical precepts" as shorthand, but they seem to be understood as a lot more than that.
It'll be wonderful: we're going to have different speakers each week.
Next week will be Talus, and there's a schedule on the website.
I also made some more copies that are in the lobby.
The talks will be followed on the subsequent Wednesday with a discussion group at 6 o'clock with that same teacher.
That's how we'll handle the fact that there isn't really time in this schedule for a lot of discussion or question and answer.
So you can save your questions, if you can remember them that long, until next week, and come a little early.
Our Bodhisattva precepts emerged originally, probably in China, as a complement to the long and very specific list of monastic precepts, generally called the Pratimoksha.
If you're not familiar with them, we have a list of 16 precepts.
The first six are very broad, and then we have 10 specific ones, and even those are in a way specific and in a way very, very broad and very simple.
The precepts include the usual things that you think of in all religious ethical systems: not killing, not stealing, being careful about your speech.
There are three of them about speech, three-tenths of the precepts are about speech, so that's important.
Being careful about sexuality, being careful about intoxicating ideas and substances, honoring the system of Buddhism itself.
So there's a little set of them, but it's quite a short list compared to the original monastic precepts, which for the monks were around 230 rules.
So there's a lot more to remember.
The nuns got extra rules, you know.
Sorry.
It's just the way it worked out, you know.
Sorry, Buddha.
Who knows what Buddha was thinking?
I don't want to make any apologies for him.
However, Buddhism was the second monastic order in world history to admit women.
The first was the Jain order, so something good happened at least.
The Catholics are still thinking about it.
We'll get there in the end.
So anyway, this original long list of rules didn't just come into being all at once.
The Buddha didn't just sit down with a pen and paper and write this long list of rules.
They came up in situations, as responses to problems.
The Buddha realized early on that how the monks and nuns conducted themselves was critical in a couple of different dimensions.
On the one hand, it's critical to their actual practice.
You can't be goofing off and causing trouble in town all day and then come home and have blissful meditation.
The mind doesn't seem to work that way.
You have to have very clear, very subtle conduct all day to support your practice, and your practice supports settled, calm, generous conduct.
So the Buddha realized that, but he also realized that it would be essential to the survival of the monastic order if they had really good relationships with the people in town.
He set it up so that they were highly dependent on the people in town.
He wanted the monastics to be able to focus full-time plus on just doing practice itself.
So it's a very simple lifestyle, and this long list of rules, the Pratimoksha rules, is a description of that lifestyle: what exactly you can possess, when you can eat, what you can eat.

It's a very strict container, and we know from our own Zen practice that a strict container may at first seem like you're losing all your freedom, but in a way it really supports a deeper kind of freedom, a freedom of being right in the middle of that structure.
In particular, in the Buddha's system, the way the monks got their food is that they would walk into town daily with their bowls and ask for food donations from the townsfolk.
They weren't going to eat if they didn't have good relationships with the town.
But this alms round wasn't just a practical matter of receiving food.
It was also a kind of exchange, a spiritual exchange, where the understanding is that the monks were supporting the practice of the lay people in town and the lay people were supporting the monks.
And the monks were also engaging in a very deep practice of equanimity and humility.
Many of the rules are around how you do that practice.
For example, at one point some of the monks had the idea, well, it would be more kind to go to the rich part of town because those people can afford it.
It probably was somewhere in the back of their minds that they would get better food.
But they were saying, well, it's better to hit the rich people up.
They can afford it more.
It's a little hard on the poor people.
So they started going only to the rich side of town, and the Buddha said, "No, no, that's no good.
You're picking and choosing in a way that's unhealthy for you and unhealthy for the lay people.
You're taking away from the people you don't visit the opportunity to practice generosity, the opportunity to participate in this vision of awakening.
So don't do that."
And the monks said, "Oh, okay, that sounds good.
We'll just go to the poor people."
And they did that.
And the Buddha said, "No, no, no, no."
So he said to them, you have to have no preference.
That'd be hard to do, wouldn't it?
Your food for the day depends on what you get.
And you're walking through Bellingham.
Are you going to go to the Lettered Streets or Edgemore?
How do you decide?
I don't know what the neighborhoods are for you if you live elsewhere from Bellingham.
Some of the rules are very simple and very practical, around their simple lifestyle.
The possessions you could own: just three robes, a sitting cloth, a begging bowl, a little medicine.
A gross side note: the medicine is specified in the Pratimoksha rule as being fermented urine.
So there's also embedded in these rules some cultural practices of the day.
I don't know what that was going to heal, but that was the medicine.
That's the permitted medicine.
Make sure you don't get sick.
Yeah, don't get sick.
They must have done other stuff too, but that's what I read.
It's in the rules.
Yeah.
So it was a real way to both simplify their lifestyle and work with materialism.
Monks and nuns also are not allowed to handle money directly.
Many monks and nuns in the Buddhist world live this way today, mostly in the southern Buddhist countries of Thailand, Burma, Sri Lanka.
There are plenty in different orders in those places, or in other Buddhist countries, who don't live that way exactly.
Buddhism is an incredibly diverse movement.
So if somebody asks you, "What do you Buddhists believe?", it's kind of a funny question, because there are many Buddhists really.
Another rule about food was no saving any food for later.
You would think, I mean that would seem practical.
What if you got something that we would keep, or it was not that hot, you could save it for later and have more time to meditate.
But no, the Buddha wanted the monks to continue practicing that engagement and that dependency and that humility with the lay people every day, no matter what.
So that's your practice every day.
Basically what you do is you get up really early and you meditate for several hours.
Then about mid-morning, once the townspeople have had a chance to get up and cook and stuff, you go on the alms round.
And then about 11 o'clock you eat a really big meal, actually.
You only eat once a day.
So [unclear: "the bulls are like, we hear bull, we think like this, the bulls are like this.
There's big things."] And then after that there would be a Dharma talk, and then practice all afternoon: walking, sitting, consulting with your seniors.
For some periods of time they practiced all night too.
So they did a heck of a lot of meditation.
Thus in the early days the communities also couldn't be too large.
You had to be very distributed, with small groups of monks and nuns coming together occasionally.
It wasn't only dependence on the individual townspeople.
The rulers of the local city-states would often support the sangha.

And the Buddha started having the custom, when it was the monsoon season and it was hard to move around, that they would come together and live a little more like what we think of as monasteries today, in bigger groups of monastics.
That would usually be sponsored by particular wealthy people who would give them big offerings and come to them.
So even still it was a little more varied than just going out on the alms round every day.
But this is what made sense and what worked in the Gangetic Plain of India in more or less the fifth century before the common era.
There are all kinds of interesting stories in the documents and writings about these early rules, about the things that went wrong and therefore we need another rule.
There was a whole rule about why you don't eat garlic, for instance.
Lots and lots and lots of them.
So very detailed.
But we didn't end up with that system.
When Buddhism moved to China, sometime between the third and the fifth centuries of the common era, the system changed.
Partly due to the climate: you probably need some more clothing if it's cold.
Partly the culture and precedent of the Chinese religions: in China it fit the culture better to establish permanent temples and monasteries.
And in order to make the monasteries work and be a little bit more self-sufficient, the monks would work in the fields.
They always tell you that, but it's only partially true, it turns out.
I'm sorry to tell you that the early, not the earliest, but the later Zen establishments were actually feudal establishments, so they had serfs too.
Unfortunately, that turns out to be true.
So all the beautiful things you hear about religion are usually not quite true.
They're still beautiful though.
They did retain, as best they could understand, many of the detailed rules of the Pratimoksha.
Some were modified for the circumstances.
But then sometime around the fifth century, the religious impulse of Buddhism started to shift in China.
This shift had been happening for many hundreds of years in India as well.
It was the coming forth of a different take on the same original teachings.
The original take was more strongly involved with personal practice, with liberation.
It was very caught up in the Indian idea of rebirth, and that being reborn is a problematic thing because you're being reborn into a place of great suffering and trouble, right, which is true.
So that was the early Buddhist idea.
The later Buddhist idea emphasized more strongly compassion and connection.
But it's not like one is really that different from the other.
It's a matter of emphasis.
So it was this later Buddhism, the Mahayana Buddhism, with more emphasis on compassion and connection, that made it to China.
Or, you know, they both made it, but that's what predominated in China.

And so the Chinese felt the need for another layer of precepts, precepts that weren't just about the individual conduct of the monastic, precepts that were more about relationship, more about connection, more about compassion.
And they did what great religious leaders have done since the beginning of time.
They created an original sutra in which the Buddha explained the additional 58 rules of the Bodhisattvas.

Of course, it was written in the fifth century, so it's a little hard to understand from a conventional historical standpoint that the Buddha could have said these things, but it was written that way.
Maybe the Buddha did say these things.
Who knows if our linear time model is all that there is.
So the Chinese invented a whole other set of precepts, and they created a sutra called the Brahma's Net Sutra.
One of the many things that's interesting about the Brahma's Net Sutra is that it purports to be a single chapter of a much longer sutra which has been lost.
So we really don't know if the longer sutra ever existed or if it was just a literary device for the Brahma's Net Sutra.
The Brahma's Net Sutra has 10 major precepts and 48 minor precepts.
What became the practice in China for the next 700 years, until Dogen showed up, the Japanese priest who founded our school, was that you did both sets of precepts.
First you did the Chinese version of the Pratimoksha rules.

So they were what we think of now as full monastics, not able to handle money except for special deals with the temple administration, living very simple full-time monastic lifestyles, although with a certain amount of working and a certain amount of modification for being in the monastic system.
The other thing that happened in China that's pretty interesting is that the Zen monastic system was state-sponsored.
So imagine that.
Whatcom County is sending us $10,000 a month and we're happily doing our thing here and most of us are full-time.
I guess they're sending us a couple hundred thousand dollars a month for us to be full-time.
So the Chinese system ended up being that way, and also of course became involved in politics, as these things go.
The precepts in Chinese Buddhism became associated with ordination.
It's unclear if that was the case in the early days of Chinese Buddhism or if that emerged during the public monastic systems which started in the seventh and eighth centuries.

As far as we know, there was a connection between ordination and precepts, but the connection became much more interwoven, and receiving the precepts became, in China, a kind of spiritual empowerment, not just a list of rules, in a way that wasn't really the case in India, as best we know.
Since the monasteries and temples became state-sponsored, the state came to control ordinations, because that's how you get in the club.
You get ordained, receive the precepts, and then you can be in the supported monastery.
The state also controlled the rotation of abbots in the large monasteries.
So it's a very different system in China than what ended up happening in Japan.
It's a big deal what exactly the precepts are, how exactly the ordination ceremony happens, and who gets to decide who the ordinee is and who the ordaining teachers are.
It's interesting.

I don't really understand how this happened exactly, but when Japan started borrowing Chinese culture in more or less the seventh century, I think, which is when Chinese writing was fully integrated into Japanese literary society, I think maybe a little earlier, they looked at these precepts as having a certain kind of esoteric power, even more than the Chinese did.
The precepts themselves became more and more an object of veneration, of empowerment, and to receive the precepts was not just an agreement to follow these rules.
It was a bringing forth of a deep connection to lineage, to Buddha himself.
It's kind of like the power of Buddha is bound up in the precepts.
One of the first major Buddhist religions to establish itself in Japan is the Tendai School of Buddhism, which is still an existing school of Buddhism in Japan.
It came from a school in China called Tiantai.
And in the Tendai system, it's pretty interesting, actually.
It's very complicated.
There are many different aspects.
They do have meditation.
They have lots of ritual, lots of chanting, lots of very old ceremonies probably dating back to India.

When we were in Japan a couple of years ago, we went to their headquarters temple and saw a monk there doing an elaborate fire ceremony, which is a goma ceremony, really, from India, and passed down over generations.
This Tendai school borrowed from all different kinds of Buddhism, and the founder of it wanted to declare his independence from China.
He wanted to establish Tendai Buddhism as an indigenous Japanese practice.

Since they saw the precepts as so powerful, how the founder, whose name is Saicho, chose to do that is he asked the emperor if he could get rid of the original long list of precepts and only ordain the monks in the Tendai school with the 58 Bodhisattva precepts from the Brahmasana Sutra.
Even in Japan, there was state control.

He had to petition the emperor for this huge change, to establish an ordination platform on Mount Hiei, their headquarters, which we visited, where the monks would receive the 58 Bodhisattva precepts and not the 200 and whatever Pratimoksha rule precepts.
This would establish a whole new monastic system, separate and independent from China.
It's hard to totally get why this would be such a huge deal, but it really was, and it took decades of negotiation.
In fact, it wasn't approved until after he died.
It was his life's work to establish this school in Japan and get this change approved.
So it's his successors who started ordaining monks with this new system.
And along comes our friend Eihei Dogen, born 1200.

He was ordained on the ordination platform at Mount Hiei with this Tendai system of 58 precepts, 10 major ones and 48 minor ones, all oriented around ethical conduct, sure, but with a sense of compassion and connection.
The theme of it is: how can we act in a way that will benefit others, not just how do I act in a way that won't cause problems and will facilitate my own awakening?
Dogen and all of the other founders of Zen and the other new Buddhisms of Japan, which emerged around that period, all started out in this Tendai school and all received this ordination.
So this is the deep backstory on our precepts.
Where did they come from?
I hope it's interesting.
I can give you a lot more information later if you're interested in studying this further.
The whole sutra is available online as well, in translation.
So thus in Japan we have this big shift in how precepts are understood.
I'm just going to read my script a little bit here because I'm losing the thread.

Starting with the eighth-century monk named Saicho, who is the founder of the Tendai school, and flowing right into the eleventh- and twelfth-century founders of Japanese Zen and Japanese Pure Land, all of whom received precepts and initial monastic training in the same Tendai school, we make two big changes.
First, we drop the Pratimoksha precepts altogether.
And second, we imbue the Bodhisattva precepts with an even more powerful religious spirit, as a great vehicle for understanding the Dharma and honoring and becoming a Buddha ancestor.
We say in our ceremonies to this day that the precepts are the blood vein of the ancestral lineage.
You get used to hearing that, but think about it for a minute.
Why would a list of rules be a blood vein of ancestors?
That's a heavy thing.
We say in our ceremonies that they're not just a support for being a better person or a wiser practitioner.
In fact, we have many teachings that say it doesn't matter how smart you are.
It doesn't matter how wise you are.
It doesn't matter how hard you try.
What matters is your deep faith in practice and precepts.
Our Dharma transmission ceremony, which is one of our holiest rituals, is completely all about this.
It's all about precepts and ancestors, mixed together in all different ways.
There are two main empowerment ceremonies in this long chain of ceremonies.
One is receiving the precepts in such a way that you can confer them.
The other is receiving the lineage of the ancestors in such a way that you become the ancestors.
There's powerful symbolism in the ceremonies, where you take the seat of Buddha and so on.
So the feeling here is that following the precepts is honoring and becoming the ancestors, that their blood is your blood.
There's even a blood-letting part of the ceremony.
No joke.
Now we do it with these little antiseptic prickers, but it must have been a knife or something.
So we have this feeling that the precepts are very central, the center of our practice.
Rules in some ways, but with a deeper spirit and meaning.
When we bring precepts to mind, when we study precepts, when we give and receive precepts in ceremonies, the feeling is that we're doing this for the ancestors.
We're not doing it for ourselves.
We're doing it for Buddha.
So then, how did we get these 16?
Remember, Dogen was ordained with 58 and all of his contemporaries were ordained with 58.
He had the sense that China was the source, that he needed to go to China to understand this new movement of Zen, which had started before him.
He was not the founder of Zen in China, but it only started about 50 years before him.

It turns out when he arrived in China, and he doesn't admit to this, but it's now pretty clear from the historians and the scholarly work, that it was a problem for him that he had this hybrid Japanese ordination.
They wouldn't let him in the door, it turns out.
He was stuck on the boat.
Somehow he got special permission to eventually join a training monastery, even though he had not received these detailed Pratimoksha precepts.
His traveling companion, another monk slightly older than him, kind of an older brother monk to him, had specially gone and received those precepts, so he was admitted sooner.
There was a place in Japan, in Nara, where you could do this, but Dogen didn't do that for some reason.
It seems clear that Dogen really was recognized by the teacher he ended up studying with, a teacher named Rujing, as a pretty special practitioner, really somebody with a deep feeling.
He was invited to have special access to the teacher, which was unusual in a big training monastery, with hundreds, maybe a thousand monks.
He got to go to a lot more private meetings with the teacher.
This is true to this day.
We think of Zen monastic training as being a very intimate teacher-student thing, and in some places it is, but not so much.
When we went to Eiheiji, the guy who gave us a little tour around had only met the abbot twice in his year and a half there.
Both times the abbot had spoken to him in very formal language that he didn't totally understand.
So it's a very ritualistic, formalized system, and a lot of the training in Zen is not about figuring something out or receiving teachings in meditation.
It's about the actual lifestyle, the way of being in the monastic container.
In Zen, they had only this short list of Bodhisattva precepts, and so they needed specific rules.
They created a whole other system for that, which are called monastic rules, rules of purity, shingyi they call them.
So the training is a training in how you live and how you do it.
Dogen somehow received special access and got to have this very intimate teacher-student relationship with his teacher, which was rare, actually.
And Dogen claims that Rujing gave him a special transmission.
I think the transmission paper exists, but the transmission paper just shows the list of ancestors.
It doesn't show the precepts he received.
He claims that Rujing gave him this special list of sixteen precepts and that from now on that's what he would transmit in his school.
This is what historians think is bogus, that it probably didn't happen.
That's interesting to think about.
On the one hand, our great founder seems to have played with the truth a little bit here in transmitting these precepts, which are partly about truthfulness, yes?
On the other hand, it also speaks to something about his deep creative vision.
I think he experienced a very deep feeling in China of what the practice was like there.
He did receive many specific ways to do things and procedures, and he set up his monastery to look like the ones he'd been in in China.
I think he had a really nuanced sense of what would work in Japan, and he somehow decided that this shorter list would be better.
So the shorter list has the first three, and this is an innovation from Dogen, we think.

The first three are taking refuge in Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, which usually is done as a separate thing, and usually a much earlier ceremony, a refuge-taking ceremony, which is how it's done in most Buddhist schools.
You would take refuge the first or second time you came here.
Sure, take refuge, great.
Sounds good to me.
Who wouldn't want Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha on their side?
But he included these refuges, and it's also a deeper thing, and the very first ever ordinations were just taking refuge.
You just say, I take refuge in Buddha, I take refuge in Dharma, I take refuge in Sangha, and the Buddha would say, okay, you're in for life.
Shave your beard.
The next three are precepts that show up in other writings as guidelines, but never as precepts.
They're basically to only do good wholesome action, to avoid unwholesome, troublesome action, and to live in relationship and connection to all beings.
So very Bodhisattva, Mahayana precepts.
And then the ten that we have are essentially the ten major precepts from this Brahma's net sutra, and he dropped the other 48.
That's what we ended up with.
Dogen never mentions anywhere, beyond claiming that he received this from Yujing, how he came up with this, and that will probably never be known.
But the great advantage that this turned out to be for the Soto Zen school in Japan was that when they had the shorter list of precepts, they got really creative with it.

They came up with a way, which had been done some, I think, in the Tendai schools, so this is a borrowing from Tendai, of using the precepts to give a sort of ordination empowerment, to give these powerful precepts to people who are lay people, who are not taking this full commitment to a lifetime of practice in the monastic container.
And what a gift.
If you understand it as this incredibly powerful, wholesome, spiritual connection to all the ancestors back to Buddha, you understand it as something that you can confer and give to somebody.
So the Soto priest could go to a village and give people this gift.
In many cases, most of the people were illiterate, and so the papers that you received from the monks would be the first time you'd seen your name written down.
So that's a powerful object, too.
This was very successful for Soto Zen.
Soto Zen spread very quickly, partly through this practice of giving precepts to lay people, which we continue to this day.
Some people in this very room have received this.
The other thing that they realized was they could also use the spiritual power of precepts in shamanistic ways.
This was, as far as I know, not done in China and India, and I don't know about other Buddhist countries.

So if there was a powerful kami, a spirit, messing things up and causing trouble in a region, the Buddhist priest would come and do a precept ceremony for these troubled spirits, offer them the wholesomeness and the spiritual power of Buddha in this way, and it would work like a charm.
So that's what we have received.
On the one hand, there are still ethical rules: not to kill, not to steal, to be kind, be careful about sex, intoxicants, and so on.
Very careful, really pay attention.
On another level, there are supports for a much deeper awareness and understanding of who we are and how we function, to take up these precepts as a way of studying our life and what we're doing.
And in another way, it's a receiving of a deep religious, spiritual connection to, sort of, beyond time, beyond time and space.
Lineage ancestors were understood to be right here in this room with us, helping us always.
So I just want to paint a little picture of the history and the matrix of it.
In the subsequent talks, myself and the other teachers are going to speak specifically about the different precepts, but to hold it with a bit of that feeling of, wow, whatever that feels like.
It's a feeling, really.
It's interesting to go to Asia and hang out with monastics there because there's a feeling.
It's not something that you can exactly explain or exactly make sense of.
Even when Dogen started doing these ordinations with these precepts, he was also just blowing off the establishment to some extent.
He was a real radical guy, and I don't know if he really could have anticipated if his school would continue.

He went off to a pretty obscure part of the mountains, several days' walk from the centers of power, with a small group of monks, and started doing these unauthorized ordinations with these unauthorized precepts.
I don't know what the political risk of that was.
Was he wondering if the imperial, whoever, were going to come and lock them all up or kill them or something?
I don't know.

Meanwhile, the other main Zen school, the Rinzai school, was mostly operating in Kyoto with the support of the power elite and only doing things, minding their Ps and Qs so they could stay in good stead.
And Dogen did not do that.
So nice for us that he did.
So that's all the time we have.
I do have a couple of handouts I'll give to you in the lobby.
One is a couple different formulations of the precepts and another is a schedule for these upcoming events.
And the third, let me just mention this too, is that several different Western, mostly American Zen teachers have written commentaries on the precepts and how to work with them.

The oldie and the bestie still is this one, I think: *The Mind of Clover* by Robert Aitken Roshi, a collection of talks he gave, I think, in maybe the late 70s, early 80s, something like that, made into a book.
I'm recommending everyone get a copy of that.
I did buy a few more copies for the library, if you can't afford to buy one.
It's out of print, but you can really get it easily on Amazon.
They come from everywhere.
Five bucks, yeah.
Five bucks, so do get a copy, if you have five bucks to spare.
Okay, so I hope that our series will be really interesting.
Some people are listening with special interest because they're starting along the path of receiving the precepts formally, which we'll talk about another night.
Thanks very much.
